newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Blast, vote remind recovering Yeltsin of problems.
newsitem.headline: Blast, vote remind recovering Yeltsin of problems.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, recovering rapidly from heart surgery, got grim reminders on Sunday from a deadly explosion and a local election defeat of problems awaiting his return to work.
Thirteen people died when a blast ripped through mourners at a memorial service in a Moscow cemetery, an apparent settling of mafia scores involving Afghan war veterans' groups.

Underlining government worries about the spread of organised crime, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin went on television to denounce a "terrorist act" and to charge Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov personally with solving the case.
Another major concern for the Kremlin as Yeltsin starts to ease himself back into power, will be the state of the economy.
Local people blamed economic problems for the heavy election defeat of Yeltsin appointee Oleg Savchenko by a communist-backed candidate for governor of the Kaluga region, south of Moscow.

Crime has risen sharply in post-Soviet Russia and Yeltsin's government has been blamed for allowing things to get out of hand. It will be a key issue on the agenda when the president, out of the Kremlin over four months, gets back to his desk.
Doctors said on Sunday Yeltsin was "satisfactory" after Tuesday's seven-hour bypass operation and was moving around more in his suite of rooms in the elite Central Clinical Hospital.
Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov told Russian Television Yeltsin could leave hospital in eight or 10 days and then go to the exclusive Barvikha sanatorium, outside the Russian capital.
In another sign of confidence in the president's entourage, both his daughters, Tatyana and Yelena, gave a light-hearted interview to NTV television, saying their father was doing well.
Yeltsin, re-elected on July 3 for a second term, has spent only a few days in the Kremlin since the poll.
Surgeon Renat Akchurin told Russian television on Saturday that doctors would remove the sutures in the next 10 or 12 days.
"He should not run, jump or play tennis, but he will be capable of talking with people, issuing orders," Akchurin said. "I have not seen a sharper mind."
Russia's social and economic situation has got much worse while Yeltsin has been away and Kremlin power struggles worsened while he waited for doctors to set a date for the operation.
The International Monetary Fund twice delayed handing over tranches of a $10 billion loan, most recently because of concerns about tax evasion and tax arrears.
Officials say the tax arrears mean the government cannot pay its bills, which in turn means workers are not paid. Tens of thousands demonstrated across Russia last week.
The economic hardships have taken their toll on Yeltsin's supporters in regional elections being held across Russia.
Kaluga's Savchenko was heavily defeated by Valery Sudarenkov, centrist who was backed by local communists.
"The main reason for Savchenko's defeat is a difficult social and economic situation in the region, delays in payment of pensions and wages and rising crime," Tass said.
Communist parliamentarian Viktor Zorkaltsev told a news conference on Sunday that the results of the election reflected "popular reaction to the deceit of July 3."
He said nine of the 19 regional elections held so far this year had been won by communist-backed candidates, seven had been won by government-backed candidates and two polls were invalid.
The final election was won by a member of extreme nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky's Liberal Democratic Party.
The local elections, being held in most of Russia's 89 regions over a six-month period ending next February, allow voters to select a new regional governor.
But the polls are important on a national level as well because the regional governors become members of the Federation Council upper house of parliament.

The State Duma lower house is already dominated by communists and their allies, who have stalled Russia's 1997 budget plans, demanding that the government rethink its revenue forecasts. The Duma is likely to discuss the budget on Friday.
